power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Developmental research has historically underrepresented families experiencing psychosocial adversity, partly due to barriers posed by in-person laboratory paradigms.
Online, webcam-based methods may support more inclusive research, but their design must be informed by the communities they seek to include.

Four focus groups were conducted with caregivers of young children (n = 10) and professionals from child protection, health, and education settings (n = 12), exploring barriers and facilitators to participation, and attitudes toward online data collection.
Transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with participant resonance checks.
Families expressed concerns about privacy and the use of children's images, while professionals described hypervigilance towards authority among multichallenged families.
Developmental feedback and resources were valued over financial incentives, and online participation was viewed favourably, conditional on material and researcher support.
Inclusive developmental science requires moving closer to families' spaces and priorities, for instance by running studies in places families already use.

Developmental science has made substantial advances in understanding early cognitive, social, and emotional development, yet this knowledge remains disproportionately drawn from families in narrow sociodemographic and cultural contexts.
Reliance on WEIRD convenience samples limits the generalisability of findings and the validity of developmental theories (Nielsen et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Reliance on WEIRD convenience samples limits the generalisability of findings and the validity of developmental theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Nielsen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Singh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This raises questions about whose experiences are represented, which contexts are treated as normative, and whether research methods are accessible and meaningful to diverse families (Broesch et al., 2023; Singh, 2024).
text.formatted: This raises questions about whose experiences are represented, which contexts are treated as normative, and whether research methods are accessible and meaningful to diverse families <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Broesch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Singh, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Families from lower-income backgrounds, younger and single parents, and minority groups are less likely to be recruited (Corr et al., 2024; Hurwitz et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Families from lower-income backgrounds, younger and single parents, and minority groups are less likely to be recruited <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hurwitz et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns appear to reflect structural conditions (such as work schedules, and distance to research facilities).

Conducting a study within early intervention centres in deprived areas, for example, yielded a considerably more diverse infant sample than a laboratory study that had specifically targeted diversity (Ballieux et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Conducting a study within early intervention centres in deprived areas, for example, yielded a considerably more diverse infant sample than a laboratory study that had specifically targeted diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ballieux et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Such conditions are particularly consequential in the first three years of life, when participation depends on caregivers balancing research with employment, household demands, and other family needs, and when their capacity to do so is shaped by access to childcare, social support, flexible work, and parental leave policies that differ across countries and social groups.

Calls to diversify infant research have therefore moved beyond recruitment towards addressing barriers embedded in research practices and infrastructure, such as how research is communicated, the accessibility of materials and procedures, and trust between researchers and communities (Garcini et al., 2022; Katus & Lloyd-Fox, 2025; Singh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Calls to diversify infant research have therefore moved beyond recruitment towards addressing barriers embedded in research practices and infrastructure, such as how research is communicated, the accessibility of materials and procedures, and trust between researchers and communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Garcini et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Katus & Lloyd-Fox, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Singh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Addressing these barriers requires rethinking the whole research process, from how questions are conceived to how engagement with communities is built and sustained, in line with their priorities and constraints (Broesch et al., 2023; Ghai et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Addressing these barriers requires rethinking the whole research process, from how questions are conceived to how engagement with communities is built and sustained, in line with their priorities and constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Broesch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Ghai et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Online methods which allow families to participate from home, may lower geographical and logistical barriers and include families for whom laboratory studies are less accessible (Zaadnoordijk et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Online methods which allow families to participate from home, may lower geographical and logistical barriers and include families for whom laboratory studies are less accessible <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Zaadnoordijk et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly relevant in Portugal, where well-equipped developmental laboratories are limited and concentrated in a few large urban centres.
However, digital methods do not automatically make research more inclusive.
As Ghai et al. (2024) noted, reaching more participants does not by itself yield a more representative sample.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ghai et al. (2024)</ref> noted, reaching more participants does not by itself yield a more representative sample.

text.text: Participation may still depend on suitable devices, internet access, digital literacy, time, and a home environment suited to assessment; video recording of young children raises privacy concerns; and technical requirements or assumptions about family routines may create new forms of exclusion.

Recent reviews of strategies to improve participation converge on facilitators such as regular contact with study staff, flexible scheduling and home or community-based options, clear communication, returning results, and appropriate compensation (Corr et al., 2024; Litchfield et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent reviews of strategies to improve participation converge on facilitators such as regular contact with study staff, flexible scheduling and home or community-based options, clear communication, returning results, and appropriate compensation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Litchfield et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The HBCD study, a large US infant neuroscience cohort, implemented participatory principles by involving child welfare professionals in community advisory boards and employing study navigators with lived experience to engage families experiencing adversity (Harden et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The HBCD study, a large US infant neuroscience cohort, implemented participatory principles by involving child welfare professionals in community advisory boards and employing study navigators with lived experience to engage families experiencing adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Harden et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In Portugal, a cohort of very preterm children achieved high retention through flexible data collection, personalised contact, supported by parents' altruistic motivation (Marques et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In Portugal, a cohort of very preterm children achieved high retention through flexible data collection, personalised contact, supported by parents' altruistic motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Marques et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, this evidence remains largely descriptive and researcher-derived, with strategies reported as what worked for a given team and little comparative evidence.
Most studies also come from North American health research and include few lowincome or multi-challenged families (Corr et al., 2024; Litchfield et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Most studies also come from North American health research and include few lowincome or multi-challenged families <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Litchfield et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Considerably less is known about how families themselves, and the professionals who support them, understand the conditions that shape participation.

Parent-informed studies are beginning to highlight accessible and transparent procedures, trust built through relationships and institutions, cultural responsiveness, and sustained presence in community settings (Marques et al., 2021; Siddiqui et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Parent-informed studies are beginning to highlight accessible and transparent procedures, trust built through relationships and institutions, cultural responsiveness, and sustained presence in community settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Marques et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Siddiqui et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Professionals supporting families cannot substitute for caregivers' perspectives, but their experience with families in diverse circumstances may help researchers anticipate concerns and adapt procedures.

To our knowledge, these perspectives remain largely absent from the literature, particularly for caregivers of infants and toddlers, in Southern European contexts, and among families in contact with child protection services.

The present study reports the first study of a larger project investigating attentional and socio-cognitive development in infants and young children across diverse geographic and psychosocial contexts in Portugal, using webcam-based online methods.

This study examined community perspectives on barriers and facilitators to participation in developmental science research, in order to shape the recruitment strategy, materials and procedures of the subsequent laboratory and home-based studies.
>Materials & Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials & Methods</head>

text.text: We conducted focus groups with two stakeholder groups.

The first comprised 10 parents of young children, and the second comprised 12 professionals working with families and young children, including professionals of social and child protection, health (e.g. nursing and paediatrics), and early childhood education.
Professionals were selected to cover a range of practice areas, including work with families exposed to adversity.
Based on an intentional sampling strategy, the participants were recruited using institutional, professional or personal networks, a recruitment flyer, email and instant messaging.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants before the start of each group discussion through an online form (Microsoft Forms), including consent to audiovisual recording.
Participants completed a brief sociodemographic questionnaire through the same form.
Sample characteristics are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: Sample characteristics are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee [blinded for review].
Recordings were stored on institutional servers and deleted after transcription verification.
Four Focus groups were conducted online via Google Meet in July 2026, two with parents, and two with professionals.
Each session lasted approximately 75 minutes.
A senior author moderated three groups and the first author one; the other acted as observer.
A semi-structured guide was developed by the research team, with parallel wording for parents and professionals.
Sessions opened with an icebreaker in which participants shared their reasons for attending, which served as a bridge to the discussion topics.

The guide then covered: (a) perceptions of or experiences with scientific research; (b) trust and privacy in the collection and use of personal data, including images and video; (c) practical and logistical barriers to participation; (d) forms of compensation considered fair and appropriate; and (e) participation in remote online studies, in which caregivers administer tasks (briefly illustrated with a video of a child completing a webcamrecorded looking task).
The guide is available in Supplementary Material S1.
Sessions were recorded and transcribed using Google Meet functions.

The first author checked each transcript against the recording and pseudonymised speakers (e.g., P1-P[n] for participants, M1-M2 for moderators) and any identifying details (e.g., names of children, services or places).
Excerpts reported were translated from European Portuguese by the authors.
In the excerpts, [...] indicates omitted text, and square brackets indicate clarifications or anonymised information added by the authors.
Excerpts are identified by participant group, focus group number and participant code (e.g., parent, P3, FG2).
Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006 , 2019; byrne, 2022), supported by NVivo Version 14.
text.formatted: Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Braun & Clarke, 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">byrne, 2022)</ref>, supported by NVivo Version 14.

text.text: We adopted a hybrid approach: coding was primarily inductive and at the semantic level, while the topics of the guide (barriers, including privacy and trust, facilitators, compensation, and online participation) provided a loose deductive frame.
Transcripts were imported with speaker and group attributes (parents vs professionals), allowing patterns to be explored within and across groups.
The first author familiarised herself with the data through repeated reading of the transcripts.
Initial coding was deliberately granular, yielding approximately 80 codes, clustered into candidate sub-themes and themes.
A second researcher with expertise in focus group methodology and thematic analysis reviewed the coding and the candidate structure.

The first author and the second researcher then met to jointly review the full coding framework, discussed each code, sub-theme, and theme, and developed a shared and consensual interpretation of the data.

During this process, codes that were redundant were removed or merged into related sub-themes, and closely related codes were combined to form new sub-themes where this better captured the pattern of meaning.
Coding coverage was used only to check whether a pattern was shared across participants and sessions rather than raised by a single participant or within a single focus group.
This process resulted in five themes and 20 sub-themes.
To check whether our interpretation resonated with participants, two first-person composite narratives, one for parents and one for professionals, were shared.
The professional narrative was voiced by a professional working with multi-challenged families, while drawing in the perspectives of colleagues from other services.
Narratives contained no verbatim quotes.

Participants received them through an anonymous online form (Microsoft Forms) with a single question on whether the story reflected what had been shared in their group, answered on a four-point scale (not at all, a little, largely, completely).
Both narratives are provided in Supplementary Material S2.

The first author is a developmental neuroscientist with experience in infant laboratory and online data collection, and the principal investigator of the project these focus groups were designed to inform.

Most participants were reached through her professional and personal networks, built through previous community-based research projects involving families and professionals working with them (e.g., in child protection and family support services).
These existing relationships facilitated recruitment and openness.
At the same time, they may have encouraged more favourable views of research.
She is also the mother of a young child, which positioned her partly as an insider in relation to the parent participants and may have shaped which accounts felt most familiar during analysis.
To mitigate these influences, three of the four sessions were moderated by a senior author with a background in psychotherapy research, therapeutic collaboration and qualitative thematic analysis.
As she is not involved in the subsequent studies of the project, she provided an outside perspective on the interpretation.
The coding framework was jointly refined between the two.
Five themes were developed: Barriers, Facilitators, Compensation, Family context as a constraint on participation, and Online modality (Table 2; Figure 1).
text.formatted: Five themes were developed: Barriers, Facilitators, Compensation, Family context as a constraint on participation, and Online modality (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In general, parent groups focused more on the facilitators whereas professionals' groups discussed more barriers, specifically those of multi-challenged families.
All ten parents and seven of the twelve professionals responded to the composite narratives.
Among parents, six rated the narrative as reflecting their group's discussion completely and four as largely.
Among professionals, six rated it as reflecting the discussion completely and one as largely.
No participant chose "a little" or "not at all".
Table 2.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: Themes, sub-themes, and theme descriptions identified in the reflexive thematic analysis of focus groups with caregivers and professionals.
This theme captures what makes families hesitant to take part, from distance to science to the practical cost of participation.
Distance between science and the community 1.2.
Concern for the child's well-being 1.3.
Concerns about privacy and use of the child's image 1.4.
Fear of judgement about the child and parenting 1.5.
Logistical and family burden 2.
Facilitators This theme describes the conditions under which participants would be more willing to take part.
Participation depended on feeling connected to the researchers, the setting and the purpose of the study.
Building trust and ongoing relationships 2.2.
Close, accessible and inviting participation settings 2.3.
Communication strategies and outreach channels 2.4.
Personal motivations to participate Theme description Sub-themes 3.
Compensation This theme covers what participants felt families should receive in return for taking part.

Their views were shaped not only by what would be attractive or fair, but also by ethical and moral considerations, such as preserving the voluntary nature of participation and the credibility and educational mission of science.
Facilitated access to healthcare and intervention 3.2.
Return of knowledge and results (individual and study) 3.3.
Educational and communitybelonging experiences 3.4.
Educational and meaningful gifts (e.g., themed book or toy) 3.5.
Divergent views on monetary compensation 4.
Family context as a constraint on participation This theme describes how a family's circumstances shape whether research feels safe or relevant.
Hypervigilance toward authority and fear of consequences 4.2.
Perceived relevance of research given family priorities 5.
Online modality
This theme captures reactions to home-based self-administered participation, which were broadly positive but conditional on support.
Before discussing this topic, participants watched a short demonstration video of a child completing a looking task on a laptop in a home-like environment with their caregiver.
Initial receptiveness to the online modality 5.2.
Challenges of caregiver-led administration 5.3.
New concerns for the child's well-being 5.4.
Technical support and guidance as facilitators Theme 1.
Barriers
Parents noted that invitations to take part in research were uncommon, and most had never heard of laboratory-based developmental studies involving infants and young children.
Some professionals noted that parents today are more receptive to evidence-based information, but that there is a gap between consuming evidence and seeing themselves as potential contributors to it.

Limited understanding of how evidence is built was seen as reducing the value the general population places on taking part in research, and one professional suggested this might be particularly marked in Portugal, where scientific literacy and engagement in science are lower.
As affirmed by a parent, "But now that I think about it, maybe for other families, I don't think it's even a matter of outreach (...)
I think it might also be a lack of interest on the part of the parents themselves" (Parent, FG4, P3).
Parents and professionals who already saw themselves as engaged with science tended to see this as an exception among the people they knew.
Scientific literacy therefore emerged as both a barrier and a facilitator (see sub-theme 2.4.).

Professionals working with multi-challenged families additionally reported that conveying the value and relevance of research to these families is particularly challenging, as their priorities often lie elsewhere (see Theme 4.2.).
As said by a professional, "It's hard for us to explain to them how useful this is.
I don't think they see it the same way." (professional, P5, FG1).
Participants worried that procedures might cause the child discomfort.

Parents said they would be reluctant to take part if they anticipated any discomfort for their child, mostly referring to emotional comfort, such as interacting with unfamiliar people in an unfamiliar environment.
As said by a parent, "If it were a study that involved the active participation of one of my children and could in some way cause them discomfort, that would be a deterrent for me" (parent, P5, FG2).
In the same line, some professionals also anticipated this reluctance among the parents they work with, in relation to both physical safety (e.g., invasive neuroimaging) and emotional discomfort.
For example, one of the professionals said: "For many parents, exposing a child to any kind of discomfort, even if it's mild, can sometimes be a challenge" (professional, P2, FG3).
This was among the most discussed barriers.
Participants feared that images could be misused or shared with third parties, and some were concerned about data security.
Parents were clear that they would share data for scientific purposes but strongly opposed any commercial or media use.
Participants also described feeling overwhelmed and uncertain about what they were consenting to, given the many data-sharing requests they face in daily life.

For most parents and professionals, however, trust in the institution mitigated these concerns, based on research ethics and the perception that institutions have had to put substantial structures in place to comply with GDPR.

For those more concerned, transparency about data management (e.g., for how long data would be kept, with a preference for keeping it for as short a time as possible), together with clear communication of its intended use, would be central to overcoming this barrier: "It's a cause for concern, of course.

I think that coming from a credible institution (…) it provides some reassurance, and also understanding, if it's made very clear in the consent form exactly what the data will be used for, who will have access to it, and where it will be stored.
I think just having that information explained clearly there already provides some reassurance, doesn't it?"
(parent, P1, FG4).
Professionals also shared experiences of parents' worries and resistance to image sharing in their own practice.
Fear of judgement about the child and parenting.
Parents and professionals described a fear that the child's or the parent's behaviour would be evaluated, so that taking part could feel like being assessed as a parent.
"I think that, in general, there's always a certain amount of uncertainty about whether we're being good parents or not.
And the fact that we're in front of researchers probably adds a little more pressure in that regard.
(…) Am I being a good parent or not?
Can I do this?"

(parent, P3, FG4) Professionals also mentioned a fear of learning something about their child or themselves that they did not wish to know, "(…) fear of being judged by others, of having issues that children might have scientifically identified, issues that parents aren't yet aware of." (professional, P4, FG3), and discussed its weight particularly for families in contact with child protection and social services (see subtheme 4.1.).
Logistical and family burden.
Both groups described travel, time, disruption of family routines and the frequency of data collection as concrete obstacles.
One professional described time concerns this way: "There's this issue of time; they're curious, but then, 'Oh, I'll have to read a lot,' or 'Oh, that takes too long.'" (professional, P4, FG4).
Work schedules were also flagged as an important constraint.

Parents who took part described themselves as privileged to have flexible working arrangements, which made them more available, but doubted that many parents around them had the same flexibility: "Maybe if it's during work hours, we might even be able to be more flexible, but that's because [partner's name] and I have that flexibility." (parent, P3, FG4) Theme 2.
Facilitators
Participants described trust as something that develops over repeated contact with the same researchers and with the institution.
Trust also depended on transparency and clear information about the study purposes and procedures.

Having a reference person was considered key, with professionals stressing that "these families' participation exist on a relationship of trust with the person extending the invitation" (professional, P3, FG1); i.e., for multi-challenged families, a trusted intermediary (e.g., a professional already known to the family) was the only way to make participation possible (see sub-theme 4.1.).
Both parents and professionals suggested that linking research to spaces families already use and trust, such as day-care centres or health centres, would be a major facilitator.

Some also proposed creating spaces designed for families, where parents and children could spend time together: "During the week there's sometimes a lot of free time that's lacking in things to do. (…) it could really be a draw if there were a sort of open-door space.

Of course, people would have to understand that they'll be evaluated or guided by someone, but it could eventually function almost like a playground, almost like a space for children to play, where they could be observed.
Of course, with everyone's knowledge." (parent, P3, FG4).
Raised only by parents, this sub-theme covers how research should reach families.

Most parents said that communicating well the purpose of a study, with a concrete picture of their contribution (which piece of the puzzle they would add), was crucial to their willingness to take part.
Recruitment through trusted networks was considered key: the paediatrician or the childcare educator, a group of parents, and social media accounts and influencers.
As one parent said "Science always ends up using much more traditional methods, doesn't it?
Now, I think we have to use the social media platforms that everyone uses, because I don't think there's any other way to reach people these days." (parent, P3, FG4).
Influencers, however, were seen as a risky channel.
The choice of person promoting a study would be decisive, and parents would accept or reject depending on whether that person's values on parenthood matched their own.
Also, some parents added that any hint of a commercial connection would lead them to decline.
Some motivations to take part were intrinsic.
Learning about their child's development and about their own parenting was a strong motivation.
Participants also valued science and the societal benefit of knowledge creation, describing a moral sense of commitment and contribution, and identification with the cause.
Scientific literacy thus appeared here as a motivator, mirroring its role as a barrier when absent (sub-theme 1.1.).

Some parents, particularly those who had previously taken part in developmental science studies, also saw participation as a fun and novel experience for both child and parent: "I also know that it can be a lot of fun, by the way, to participate in experiments and studies with children." (parent, P4, FG4).
This view surprised parents without such experience: "I hadn't thought of it that way, but it could be fun, right?
Just another activity, going there, and they get to experience it too, don't they?"
(parent, P2, FG4).
This suggests that presenting research participation as a playful shared experience could make participation more attractive.
Theme 3.
text.formatted: <head>Theme 3.

text.text: Compensation
text.formatted: Compensation</head>

text.text: Mentioned mainly by professionals, this referred to participation as a route to developmental screening, referral or support.

In the words of one professional: "Anything related to interventions, partnerships with clinics that can help children with certain difficulties; that's what would make the most sense" (professional, P7, FG1).
Discounts on treatments, or access to innovative interventions or multidisciplinary expert teams from academic settings, were seen as attractive forms of compensation.

Participants valued information and training on the study topic, feedback on their own child, and a summary of the study's findings, The latter mattered because they wanted that their contribution was recognised as part of building something larger.
As one professional put it: "Access to the results of that study would also be very important, because sometimes people participate and have absolutely no idea what happened.
And I think people could know that they're taking part in something, but also that they'll get to know the result.
I think that, in the future, it might even make people more willing to participate in new projects and everything else." (professional, P3, FG3)

Professionals and parents were very positive about cultural or educational activities as compensation, such as a family ticket to the zoo or a museum, that could also offer families a shared experience.
Participants felt this aligned well with the educational mission of science.
Participants also suggested creating a network of participating families, for example through a gathering at the end of the study.
As said, "Also having a chance to share with other families, to feel included.
I think so, that would be one of the things families usually really enjoy." (professional, P1, FG3).
This was seen as a form of return that promotes a sense of identity with research and ongoing relationships, which in turn facilitates future participation.
A themed book or toy was valued as a thoughtful choice, for its educational and meaningful value.
Both groups appreciated when the item was related to the research topic and accompanied by evidence-based information on that topic (related to sub-theme 3.2.).
For example, a professional said: "In my view, an educational kit, a kit of activities designed to stimulate or raise awareness among families" (professional, P3, FG1).
This was the most contested topic.
Some professionals saw financial compensation as fair, both as a way of making participation accessible to families with fewer resources and as recognition of time taken from work or household tasks.
However, other professionals and some parents expressed moral discomfort.

They worried that payment could compromise the authenticity and voluntariness of participation, as well as the institution's credibility and the educational and transformative mission of science: "Personally, if they told me about that, I wouldn't sign up.
If they mentioned a voucher, I think it would lose its scientific credibility for me." (professional, P1, FG3).

Some also noted that financial compensation could be perceived as a commercial transaction or conflict of interest, which would deter them from taking part: "I would probably immediately think that the study was being paid for by some brand behind the study, and so, for me, (…), that wouldn't be a positive thing" (parent, P4, FG2).
Material goods (e.g., nappies, wipes, a snack at the end of the research visit) or a justification for work absence were suggested as a middle ground.
Theme 4.
Family context as a constraint on participation 4.1.
Hypervigilance toward authority and fear of consequences.

Professionals working with families followed by child protection or social services described these families as living with constant hypervigilance and anxiety about being judged as parents and about the consequences for their family.
As one professional explained: "They are naturally hypervigilant.
So they will always think, no matter how much you explain that it's not the case. that it might have some kind of consequence" (professional, P5, FG1).
Families might fear that what is observed in a study could be reported, used against them, or escalate their child protection process.

Professionals worried that, if recruitment through protection services, families could feel unable to refuse or would not separate research from their support process, compromising voluntary participation.
At the same time, professionals were firm that a reference person already close to the family was the only viable route to recruitment and engagement (see sub-theme 2.1.).

This points to a tension between the role of trusted professionals as facilitators of participation and the risk that their involvement may compromise its voluntary nature and reinforce families' fears.

Professionals working with multi-challenged families reported that these families find it difficult to see the added value of research, as their priority is resolving day-to-day challenges (sometimes unmet basic needs).
A professional described it this way: "One obstacle to participation is the question of what is truly a priority and relevant to these people, isn't it?

Because in a context of vulnerability, participating in a scientific study, the benefit of doing so, is perhaps something that most people cannot grasp; they cannot see how their lives are actually positively impacted by being part of this type of research" (professional, P4, FG1).

In contrast, professionals working outside the child protection system described a strong curiosity among today's parents to learn about their children and about parenting, and an active search for evidencebased knowledge: "Most are interested in consuming, so to speak, science; that is, they're interested in knowing the results of their practices in scientific terms, and they understand this very well." (professional, P2, FG3).
As highlighted in Theme 1, parents similarly felt that openness to scientific knowledge and participation would depend on a family's scientific literacy and work demands.
Theme 5.
Online modality
Both groups reacted positively at first.

Online sessions were seen as reducing burden (no travel, shorter sessions, asynchronous completion) and as more comfortable and safe for the child, with the caregiver leading the session in a familiar environment.
One professional framed the participation as play like this: "I think parents would love it too, because I also think it's fun for them.
It's a way for them to play with their child, I think.
And I think the kid, the child, isn't aware that they're being studied; they're just playing." (professional, P1, FG3).

Participants anticipated difficulties related to digital literacy and technical problems (e.g., internet connection, browser compatibility), access to suitable equipment (e.g., a laptop), and insecurity about running tasks without a researcher present (including the fear of facing technical issues).

The latter is illustrated by a parent: "I think it would be the fear that the technology might fail, and then I'd be there alone at home, and suddenly it's not working, and the computer isn't working, and that's it." (parent, P4, FG4)
The online format raised its own barriers.
Participants worried that child's cooperation at home would be dependent on the child's temperament.
A professional warned that "Just having the child sit in front of a screen to participate could already be a bit complicated" (professional, P7, FG1).
Screen time was another concern: both parents and professionals described strict limits in current family routines.
Finally, privacy concerns extended to the family home.
Participants suggested that the presence of a support researcher or intermediary (remotely or in person), and clear instructions via demonstration videos would facilitate online participation.

Participants also suggested making the format more flexible, for example through a platform where parents could return several times to complete trials, rather than going through the whole task in one session.
This was seen as less demanding for both parents and children.

For professionals, an in-person facilitator (e.g., a researcher visiting the home to run the task, or setting up the study within a service) remained crucial for participation of multi-challenged families, as explained by one professional: "The presence of someone in the home, someone from the research team, could help unlock situations where families either don't have the equipment or don't feel so comfortable carrying out the task." (professional, P5, FG1).
The current study explored how caregivers and professionals in Portugal perceive families' participation in developmental research.

Across five themes (barriers, facilitators, compensation, family context as a constraint on participation, and online modality), our findings suggest that participation depends on trust, perceived safety, and the fit between research and families' circumstances.
Privacy concerns over the use of children's images were a salient barrier to parents; hypervigilance towards authority was raised only by professionals.
Parents' discussions focused on motivation, communication, and trust, whereas professionals focused on structural constraints, hypervigilance, and compensation.

This difference likely reflect proximity: professionals working with multi-challenged families see constraints that may be less visible among focus group parents, who likely represent more research-ready families.
Across themes, participants linked participation to intermediaries' or researcher's trust and presence in places families use.
Participants described a distance between science and families and pointed to closer, accessible, and engaging spaces where families could encounter research as part of their everyday lives.

Such spaces, designed for parents and children to spend time together, could double as settings for science dissemination and knowledge exchange, where taking part in research becomes a way for parents to learn about their child, and thus a form of compensation in itself. Siddiqui et al. (2026) also identified trust built through institutions, health professionals, and sustained presence in children's centres and community settings. Corr et al. (2024) and Litchfield et al. (2026) similarly found that familiar venues, culturally attuned community events, and continuity of contact with the same researcher supported recruitment.

(2026)</ref> also identified trust built through institutions, health professionals, and sustained presence in children's centres and community settings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Corr et al. text.text: In Portugal, Marques et al. (2021) reported that face-to-face contact with the people behind a study mattered to families.
text.formatted: In Portugal, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Marques et al. (2021)</ref> reported that face-to-face contact with the people behind a study mattered to families.

text.text: Whereas logistical constraints dominate much of the literature, privacy was a key barrier to our participants.
This salience partly reflects our design, as privacy was a prompted topic and we highlighted the role of video-based methods in developmental neuroscience.
Nonetheless, participants' concerns were specific: uncertainty about where data might travel, fear of data leaks, and a wish for data minimisation and timely erasure.
Similar privacy concerns have been reported (Corr et al., 2024; Siddiqui et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similar privacy concerns have been reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Siddiqui et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These expectations conflict with common research practice.

Scientific and ethical considerations favour maximising each family's contribution, and in underfunded research systems there are strong incentives to collect more data than a single study requires and to retain them for future use.
Infant video data are costly to obtain and valuable for secondary analyses but cannot be fully anonymised.
Reconciling these positions will likely require stating openly who can access recordings, for how long, and for what purposes, so that families can make informed choices about reuse.
Hypervigilance towards authority appeared only in professionals' accounts.
This is likely due to self-selection, as the families described were unlikely to join parent focus groups.
However, this converges with fear of child protection involvement reported among parents who use substances (Corr et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, this converges with fear of child protection involvement reported among parents who use substances <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Professionals stressed that while they can open access to families who are otherwise hard to reach, recruitment through services with authority over families risks compromising voluntariness.
Researchers should state explicitly that participation is separate from case management and describe safeguarding procedures (including mandated reporting) transparently at consent.
Community spaces not tied to authority-holding services might offer a lower-threat entry point, with professionals inviting families into these spaces; however, our data do not test this directly.

Consistent with Harden et al. (2024), who argue that families facing multiple adversities need intensified rather than different strategies, professionals pointed to clearer explanation of research benefits, deeper relationship-building with families and their practitioners, flexible venues, and more thoughtful compensation.
text.formatted: Consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Harden et al. (2024)</ref>, who argue that families facing multiple adversities need intensified rather than different strategies, professionals pointed to clearer explanation of research benefits, deeper relationship-building with families and their practitioners, flexible venues, and more thoughtful compensation.

text.text: Views on monetary compensation diverged.
Some participants saw payment as fair recognition and a means of accessibility; others feared it compromised voluntariness and the credibility of science.

The most attractive returns were non-monetary: knowledge about the child and study results, educational and community experiences, and resources such as books and toys. Ballieux et al. (2016) found that gaze replay was particularly valued by lower-SES parents, suggesting a concrete return for eye-tracking studies such as ours.
text.formatted: The most attractive returns were non-monetary: knowledge about the child and study results, educational and community experiences, and resources such as books and toys. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ballieux et al. (2016)</ref> found that gaze replay was particularly valued by lower-SES parents, suggesting a concrete return for eye-tracking studies such as ours.

text.text: Although not explored directly, combining small returns (travel and childcare reimbursement, feedback on results, a souvenir such as gaze replay or a photograph of the infant in the research setting, and a modest material item or experience) may be fairer and more inclusive than any single form.

The distance we found between science and families, and the motivations described (learning about development and parenting, fun for the child, valuing science) show that participation is attractive when families see the benefit of it.
Framing participation as an opportunity for parents to learn about and connect with their child may make research feel less like a duty and more like a shared experience.

Precedents include "Learn About Your Baby" sessions in Children's Centres (Ballieux et al., 2016), laboratory playdates (Brand et al., 2019), and home-like research spaces with snacks and toys (Harden et al., 2024). Litchfield et al. (2026) likewise found that families preferred safe and friendly venues over clinical settings, with higher recruitment at community events.

(2026)</ref> likewise found that families preferred safe and friendly venues over clinical settings, with higher recruitment at community events.

text.text: For communication, participants pointed the importance of making the concrete relevance of studies clear, and to social media as a channel (consistent with Siddiqui et al., 2026), with caution regarding influencers, whose values had to match their own.

text.text: Participants were initially receptive to online participation, citing lower logistical burden, comfort at home, the caregiver leading the session, and its playful character.
Participation depended on digital literacy and access to materials, and new concerns arose about the child's cooperation, screen time, and privacy at home.
Facilitators included a support researcher or intermediary, shorter repeatable sessions, and demonstration videos.

Intuitive participation flows may help caregivers feel confident running the tasks, while playful, game-like structures could make participation more rewarding, encouraging families to take part and to return.

Because online tasks do not depend on a fixed setting, they could also be run in other venues, such as community spaces or services families already attend, with a researcher or trusted professional present.
Families could then choose where to take part according to their needs and preferences.

Such flexibility may be especially important for low-income and multichallenged families: Hurwitz et al. (2017) let families choose between home, lab or library sessions to accommodate work schedules, transport and sibling care.
text.formatted: Such flexibility may be especially important for low-income and multichallenged families: <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hurwitz et al. (2017)</ref> let families choose between home, lab or library sessions to accommodate work schedules, transport and sibling care.

text.text: This study has several strengths.

Combining caregivers' and professionals' perspectives allowed us to identify shared and distinct views, such as hypervigilance towards authority, which emerged only in professionals' accounts and would have been missed with parents alone.
Including child protection professionals was particularly valuable, as they offered insight into the circumstances of families who rarely take part in research.
The study also addresses a Portuguese context that is underrepresented in the literature, which has been dominated by North American and Northern European samples.

Finally, the interpretation was developed collaboratively by two researchers with different backgrounds and checked with participants using composite narratives, extending participants' engagement to the interpretation stage, which is still uncommon in the literature (Wagman et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Finally, the interpretation was developed collaboratively by two researchers with different backgrounds and checked with participants using composite narratives, extending participants' engagement to the interpretation stage, which is still uncommon in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Wagman et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations should also be considered.

Parents who volunteered for focus groups were likely more research-engaged than the broader population, and their views may underrepresent the barriers faced by families who are less familiar with research.
Although professionals helped to bridge this gap, they spoke on behalf of families, and their accounts may reflect their own professional frameworks.
Findings may not transfer directly beyond the Portuguese context, given differences in research culture, service structures, and data protection norms.
Finally, our discussions focused on initial participation, and retention in longitudinal studies was not addressed.
Future work should include families recruited through community rather than research channels and examine how perceptions change once families have taken part.

• Sharing research in trusted community venues and creating or repurposing family spaces (community centres, libraries, health centres) as hubs for dissemination, knowledge exchange, and participation, including as entry points to online studies; • Communicating transparently about data and image policies addressing minimisation and retention; • Engaging intermediaries as partners who invite families to participate, with research clearly separated from case management; • Implementing online protocols that allow caregiver-, intermediary-, or experimenter-led setups; • Designing compensation mixing knowledge return, practical goods, and cost coverage.

In our study, caregivers and professionals described participation as valued when research was credible and close to families (through institutional credibility, trusted intermediaries, and a presence in communities) and when it offered something meaningful in return (a clear purpose, the return of knowledge, and perceived benefit to the child).

At the same time, concerns about privacy and the use of children's images, hypervigilance towards authority among families in adversity, and competing day-today priorities show that these conditions are not equally met for all families.

Inclusive developmental science therefore requires bringing science into the spaces where families live and play, so that taking part in research becomes part of how families learn about and enjoy their children.
For online developmental science, this involves transparent data practices, human support for remote participation, and sustained community presence.
Such approaches, particularly with underserved families, demand time and resources that current funding models rarely accommodate.
Funders and policymakers should recognise the investment needed to bring developmental science closer to families (Litchfield et al., 2026; Wagman et al., 2025).
